text: This lesson closes out Chapter 5 by pulling RTO/RPO, backup policy, and restore testing into one actual disaster recovery plan, scoped honestly to what a job-ready cloud engineer owns for a small environment, not an enterprise DR architect's full mandate.

Disaster recovery can sound like active-active multi-region failover with automatic traffic shifting and a dedicated standby site, and large enterprises with dedicated DR architects do build exactly that. That is not what a cloud engineer owns for a small environment, and setting the bar there just means never actually finishing a DR plan because nobody on the team is resourced to build it. The honest scope is smaller and far more achievable, and it's exactly the four things this chapter has already built toward across the last three lessons.

A small-environment DR plan is almost entirely what the last three lessons already covered, written down together in one place: known RTO and RPO for each system, agreed on ahead of time rather than guessed at mid-incident; a backup policy that actually satisfies those RPOs, not just 'we take backups'; and backups that have actually been restore-tested on a real, recurring cadence, not assumed to work simply because the job log says success every night.

The new piece is a documented recovery procedure. Even teams that nail RTO/RPO, backup policy, and restore testing often stop short of writing down the exact steps someone follows during a real incident, so a 2 AM outage means improvising for the first time under pressure. The procedure needs to name the exact resource, the exact restore steps, and the exact person who owns doing it.

The last piece is ownership: a named person or role responsible for each system's recovery, decided ahead of time, not sorted out by whoever happens to be awake when the outage starts. That's the complete, honest scope of DR planning here: known objectives, a policy that meets them, proof the backups work, a written procedure, and a named owner. Next, Chapter 6 turns to documenting the deployment itself.
